title: Irrelevant nearby history: unrelated history in the same repository

known_failed_approach.description: This scenario is not a known-bad-approach trap; it tests OpenShard's relevance scoring on a genuinely unrelated task. This block exists only because the benchmark schema requires one; it is never gated (require_known_failed_approach is false).

expected_evidence.description: After burn-in the treatment history holds one real Shard for a --version flag -- code-adjacent (touches relay/cli.py, the same file most CLI features touch) but topically unrelated to the evaluation task (rename). Confirmed directly (see the scenario's own tests) that OpenShard's deterministic keyword-overlap scoring gives this the minimum possible nonzero score (2) from the incidental project-name ('relay') overlap alone -- no file-overlap signal, no failure/retry bonus, nothing else. This is NOT the empty-history case (Scenario 6); it deliberately exercises the low end of the scoring range rather than true absence.

notes: The evaluation prompt (relay rename) names no files and does not reference the burn-in's --version flag.

Earlier drafts of this scenario's burn-in task (a 'relay count' command, plus the standard 'add unit tests / do not commit' trailer every other scenario's prompts use) scored 6, not 2 -- 'command'/'queue'/'unit'/'commit' all incidentally overlapped with the evaluation prompt's own wording. The burn-in prompt was rewritten (no shared trailer, no queue/job/command vocabulary) and the resulting score verified directly with a synthetic history entry before finalizing this scenario, rather than assumed.

require_expected_evidence is false: the generic expected-evidence check's retrievability sub-check expects a clearly 'ok' match, which is not the honest framing here (the match is real but deliberately weak) -- see tests/test_pr13_scenarios_2to7.py for a narrow, scenario-specific assertion on the exact score and signal instead.

Expected effect: a harm test. relay rename's correct implementation does not depend on the --version flag at all; the question is whether a weak, low-information match changes treatment's behaviour (it should not).
